newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-OBERHOLZER REFLECTS ON MIXED FIRST YEAR-.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-OBERHOLZER REFLECTS ON MIXED FIRST YEAR-.

text.p: It has been the best of times and the worst of times for South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) chief executive Rian Oberholzer.
With the British Lions due this Sunday, the problems continue for Oberholzer after a turbulent first year in office.

A government task force is investigating allegations of financial irregularities in the running of South African rugby, a fourth player awaits sentencing for alleged steroid abuse while a disaffected rump of coloured and black administrators from the pre-unification rugby boards threaten to boycott the Lions tour.
"I would be lying if I said there weren't times I said 'is it really worth my while to keep banging my head against the wall?'," the fresh-faced 36-year-old Oberholzer said in an interview this week.
"It was a difficult year and a hard year. We went through lots of crises and problems but we kept focused and in the end we achieved our goals. But it was tough."
Oberholzer can claim many successes in his first year.

The game now has a professional system modelled on English soccer in place and more non-whites are now playing. On the field the Springboks ended the year with six successive test victories, five of them away from home.
But it is the litany of public relations disasters for which Oberholzer's first year will be remembered.

Brian van Rooyen, a Johannesburg accountant and coloured vice-president of the former Transvaal Rugby Union (now the Gauteng Lions), compiled a 500 page dossier suggesting irregularities in the financial dealings of SARFU and the Lions and questioned the use of money earmarked for rugby development projects.
The dossier led to the establishment in February of a government task force which has yet to report.

Three days later, the game was embroiled in an even more explosive and shaming furore when a tape recording was released of Springbok coach Andre Markgraaff making a racist attack on black sports administrators.
Markgraaff resigned two days later -- pre-empting the impending sack -- but rugby had suffered another fearful body blow.
"The people involved in it don't realise how much they hurt South African rugby," said Oberholzer.
"They turn around and say they did it for the good of the game but I would like them to explain to me how it is good for the game to tape a guy and then try and sell it.

"Van Rooyen sat on a document for months and when it came out it was nothing. Van Rooyen is now threatening to try and stop the Lions tour coming to South Africa. How does he serve the game by doing that?"

In July, before Oberholzer's first month in the job had been completed, the selection of hooker Henry Tromp and the reappearance of South Africa's apartheid era flag among rugby fans wiped out the advances made during the nation-building World Cup victory of the previous year.
Tromp and his father had been tried for manslaughter following the death of a 16-year-old black farm worker and his selection by Markgraaff seemed, at best, politically insensitive.
Tromp sat on the bench in the Tri-Nations test against Australia in Bloemfontein in July when the old South African flag conspicuously re-appeared among fans.

The presence of the blue, white and orange apartheid emblem was immediately condemned by Springbok manager Morne du Plessis but a row erupted when skipper Francois Pienaar said supporters were welcome with any flag.
SARFU were slow to issue their own condemnation and it was only months after his call-up that SARFU belatedly disclosed that Tromp's selection had been cleared with President Mandela's office.

South Africa's subsequent first home series defeat by New Zealand in August deepened the gloom while there was a heated public debate over the dropping of popular wing James Small for visiting a night club visit on the eve of a test and the disclosure that coloured government finance minister Trevor Manuel cheered for the All Blacks against the all-white Springboks.
Worse was to follow in October. There was a national outcry when Pienaar, the World Cup winning national captain, was dropped for the end of season tour to Argentina, France and Wales.
The perception was that rugby was trying to turn back the political clock by axing Pienaar, who learned from journalists that he had been omitted.
"We hurt ourselves in the manner we handled the Francois Pienaar case. That wasn't professionally done -- we should have handled it differently," conceded Oberholzer.
"The whole flag issue was also badly handled and we had the Henry Tromp thing. There's many things we may have done differently but we do make mistakes."

Remarkably, considering SARFU's year, Oberholzer has not been subject to any personal criticism. He has steered South Arican rugby into the professional era putting in place regulations on transfers, drugs, disciplinary procedures and new management structures.
"We got rid of a lot of old ideas and we are changing mindsets especially at provincial level," he said.
"On the professional side I leaned heavily on British football. They have made, and corrected, all their mistakes so why do we need to reinvent the wheel if there's a system in place?

"I spent some time at Newcastle United looking at their structures but the world is so small on the Internet. I picked up the transfer regulations from the F.A. (Football Association), how they treat their referees, all from the Internet.
"At the time of the European championships I printed off all their doping regulations and compared them with ours. English football was a good model for us to follow."
Oberholzer is hoping for a more serene second year at SARFU's Cape Town headquarters and remains optimistic for the future of the South African game.
"I kept thinking 'when am I going to start having some fun around here?' But there's a lot of excitemnt and there's a lot great people around you who share the vision," he said.
"In 10 years' time the majority of the Springbok team will be players of colour but my vision is twofold.

"I want ours to be the most professionally run sporting body in South Africa and secondly we must be able to give everyone who wants to play the game of rugby an opportunity to compete on an equal footing.
"It sounds very simplistic but if we can achieve that we will really have done something."
